background.heading: Engineering first, then code
paragraphs: I hold a degree in Mining Engineering from the University of Belgrade (graduated 2010). In 2026 the Bavarian Chamber of Engineers (Bayerische Ingenieurekammer-Bau) found my education equivalent to German requirements and granted me the professional title Ingenieur.

I started in 2011 as a mining engineer on mineral exploration projects, including underground work, then moved into drilling in 2012, planning and supervising exploration wells. Since 2013 I have worked in coiled tubing and nitrogen operations, from field engineer to operations manager, on more than 1,000 jobs. That work taught me how real operations behave: pressures, limits, and what breaks when a number is wrong. I bring that habit of checking the numbers into every website and tool I build.
For technical companies this means less explaining. You do not have to teach me what a job looks like on site before I can build the page for it.

meta.title: CT Strength Limits
meta.description: Check coiled tubing against burst, collapse and tension: stresses, von Mises equivalent stress and API collapse and burst limits, in oilfield or metric units.

hero.title: CT Strength Limits
hero.description: Stresses, burst, collapse and tension limits of coiled tubing for the load you enter, with the von Mises check against the yield factor. Oilfield or metric units.

ovality.label: Ovality
ovality.hint: (ODmax − ODmin) / OD; about 0.005 for new tubing

yieldStress.label: Yield strength
yieldStress.hint: Minimum yield strength of the steel

yieldFactor.label: Yield factor
yieldFactor.hint: Design factor on the yield strength

axialForce.label: Axial force
axialForce.hint: Positive in tension, negative in compression

bendingRadius.label: Bend radius
bendingRadius.hint: Radius the tubing is bent over; 0 for straight tubing

safetyFactor.label: Collapse safety factor
safetyFactor.hint: Safety factor of the API 5C7 collapse correction for tension, at least 1

method.title: Method
method.intro: The tubing is checked as a thick-walled steel tube under internal and external pressure, axial force and an optional bend.
steps: Axial stress is the axial force over the steel area. A bend of radius R adds the bending stress E·OD/(2R) on the convex side and subtracts it on the concave side; the larger absolute value is used.

Hoop and radial stress at the inside wall come from the Lamé equations for a thick cylinder; the radial stress there equals minus the internal pressure. The von Mises stress combines the three: √(σa² + σh² + σr² − σa·σh − σa·σr − σh·σr). Torque is not included.

Burst: API 5C3 internal yield 0.875 · 2Y·t/D; capped-end yield (4Y/√3)·(t/D)·(1 − t/D), where the von Mises stress at the inside wall reaches Y; true burst (2Y/√3)·ln(OD/ID), where the whole wall yields.

Collapse: Timoshenko, Pc = [Py·R + Pe·(1 + 3·ov·D/2t) − √((Py·R + Pe·(1 + 3·ov·D/2t))² − 4·Py·Pe·R)] / 2, with Py = 2Y·t/D, Pe = 2E/(1 − ν²)·(t/D)³ and R the reduction for axial stress; round tubing has ov = 0. API 5C3 uses the yield, plastic, transition or elastic range of D/t, with the yield strength reduced for axial stress. API RP 5C7 gives the collapse of oval tubing from the round collapse and the ovality, and in tension reduces it by Kcf = ((1/SF)^(4/3) − (L/Ly)^(4/3))^0.75.
Tension limits: Ly = yield factor · Y · steel area, and the largest axial force that keeps the von Mises stress at the yield factor with the hoop and radial stress of the entered pressures.
assumptions: A seamless steel tube with uniform wall and the nominal dimensions entered, without corrosion, wear or fatigue.
Pressures are uniform along the tubing; the stresses are those at the inside wall, the worst case.
Torque and shear stresses are not included.
The API collapse equations are valid for the D/t range of the standards; check results outside it.
method.reference: Based on the API 5C3 and API RP 5C7 equations, Timoshenko collapse, the Lamé equations and the von Mises criterion. The calculation reproduces a reference worksheet for its example case. Check the standards before you rely on a result; fatigue life is not covered.

meta.title: Nitrogen Displacement
meta.description: Calculate how much nitrogen is needed to displace the fluid in a well through coiled tubing: gas at standard conditions, as liquid nitrogen and by mass, in metric or oilfield units.

hero.title: Nitrogen Displacement
hero.description: How much nitrogen it takes to displace the fluid in a well through coiled tubing, including the tubing still on the reel. Metric or oilfield units.

ctLength.label: Coiled tubing on the reel
ctLength.hint: Total length, including what goes into the well

depth.label: Pumping depth
depth.hint: Depth the nitrogen is pumped from

fluidDensity.label: Fluid in the well
fluidDensity.hint: Density of the fluid being displaced

compressibility.label: Compressibility factor, Z
compressibility.hint: 1 for an ideal gas; nitrogen at high pressure is higher, from a gas table

nitrogenDensity.label: Mean nitrogen density in the well
nitrogenDensity.hint: Average density of the gas column; sets the pressure at the wellhead

results.title: Result
results.reel: Filling the tubing on the reel

method.title: Method
method.intro: The well fluid is displaced down to the pumping depth; the nitrogen that fills the column, and the tubing left on the reel, is totalled as gas, liquid and mass.
steps: Pressure at depth balances the hydrostatic column of the well fluid: P = ρ·g·h. The wellhead pressure is that minus the weight of the nitrogen column, from the mean nitrogen density. The column is taken at the mean of the two pressures and of the two temperatures.
Volume factor of nitrogen: B = 2.8416·P / (Z·(273 + T)) in sm³/m³, with P in kPa and T in °C. The constant stands for standard conditions of about 15 °C and 101.3 kPa.
Volume filled with gas: the production tubing bore minus the coiled tubing steel, times the depth. That is the annulus and the coiled tubing bore, each counted once.
Nitrogen for the well is that volume times the factor at mean conditions. Nitrogen for the tubing still on the reel is its bore volume times the factor at wellhead conditions.
Liquid nitrogen: 1 m³ of liquid gives 696.5 sm³ of gas and weighs 808 kg.
assumptions: The fluid is displaced completely down to the pumping depth, in a vertical well.
The compressibility factor is constant along the column; the temperature is the mean of the two ends.
The mean nitrogen density is an input, not derived from the pressure, so the wellhead pressure follows from it.
No fluid enters the well and no nitrogen is lost; nothing is allowed for the pumping losses or a reserve.
method.reference: Reproduces a reference worksheet, with one difference: the worksheet counts the coiled tubing bore twice in the volume filled with gas, which here is counted once, so the nitrogen for the well is lower than the worksheet’s. Check the gas properties against a nitrogen table before you rely on a result.

meta.title: CT Pressure Loss
meta.description: Calculate the friction pressure loss of a power-law fluid pumped through coiled tubing, split into straight and reel-wound sections, in oilfield or metric units.

hero.title: CT Pressure Loss
hero.description: Frictional pressure loss for power-law fluids pumped through coiled tubing. Enter the fluid, the tubing and the flow rate, in oilfield or metric units.

n.label: Flow behaviour index, n
n.hint: Power-law exponent; 1 for a Newtonian fluid

k.label: Consistency index, K
k.hint: Power-law consistency, from the rheology of the fluid

reelDiameter.label: Reel diameter
reelDiameter.hint: Diameter of the coil the tubing is wound on

roughness.label: Wall roughness
roughness.hint: Absolute roughness of the inside wall; 0 for smooth tubing. Only affects turbulent flow

lengthOffReel.label: Tubing off the reel
lengthOffReel.hint: Straight length, not wound on the reel

method.title: Method
method.intro: The loss is calculated separately for the part of the string off the reel (straight) and the part on the reel (curved), and the two are added.
steps: Reynolds number (Metzner–Reed): Re = 31.042 ρ Q^(2−n) / (9.804^n K ID^(4−3n)) · (n/(1+3n))^n, with ρ in lb/gal, Q in gal/min, ID in inches and K in lbf·sⁿ/100 ft².
Straight tubing: laminar below Re = 3470 − 1370n and turbulent above 4270 − 1370n. Laminar f = 16/Re. Turbulent f = a/Re^b, with a = (log n + 3.93)/50 and b = (1.75 − log n)/7.

Coiled tubing: the laminar factor is multiplied by ψ·De^φ, where De = Re_g·(ID/D)^0.5 is the Dean number, ψ = 47.969 − 153.8n + 166.22n² − 60.132n³ and φ = 0.875n − 0.515. Turbulent: f = 1.069·a/Re^(0.8b)·(ID/D)^0.1. The laminar limit is (4n/(3n+1))^n · [2100 ψ (ID/D)^(0.5φ)]^(1/(1−φ)) and the turbulent limit is 800 above it.

Pressure loss: ΔP = f ρ Q² L / (154.63 ID⁵) in oilfield units. Between the two limits the loss is interpolated linearly in Re, from the laminar loss at the lower limit to the turbulent loss at the upper limit.
assumptions: Wall roughness enters only the turbulent friction factor, as the ratio of the Haaland factor with roughness to the one without, so a roughness of 0 gives the smooth-tube result. For n other than 1 this is an estimate.
A single-phase power-law fluid without solids.
Smooth tubing and fully developed flow, with fluid properties constant along the string.
The curvature is that of the reel diameter you enter; tubing off the reel is straight.
The correlations cover a limited range of n and ID/D. Check results outside it.
method.reference: Based on published correlations for power-law fluids in coiled tubing (Zhou and Shah), with the Metzner–Reed Reynolds number and Dodge–Metzner turbulent factors. The calculation reproduces a reference worksheet for its example case. Check the original papers before you rely on a result.
